units: a resident from an upper floor tells the caretaker about a door that no longer locks
the catch gives way as soon as the handle is let go
water comes in through a damaged drainpipe above the door
the caretaker had already written the fault down in his logbook
he says he can do nothing without approval from the building manager
the resident points out that the delay is helping the lock to rust
the two agree to hold the door leaf with a wooden wedge
a sheet is to be used to send the water across to the street drain
the caretaker promises a written reminder before the week is out
the resident wants to gather written backing from the other occupants
text: A resident from one of the upper floors stopped the caretaker to report that the cycle store door would no longer lock. The catch, she said, slipped back the moment the handle was let go, and water was coming in through a split drainpipe above the doorway. The caretaker replied that the fault was already down in his logbook, though he could take no action until the building manager approved it. Waiting only helped the rust along, she pointed out, and the lock would seize before long. Between them they settled on a temporary measure: a wooden wedge would hold the leaf shut, and a sheet of canvas would carry the water across to the street drain. The caretaker undertook to send a written reminder before the week was out. She, for her part, offered to collect written backing from the other occupants.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: households once drew their water from a dug shaft or from a tank
you had to haul a vessel up and wait for the grit to settle at the bottom
the supply was kept in an earthenware pot standing somewhere cool
these days one movement at the household fitting brings the water
the flow no longer depends on the bodily strength of whoever draws it
the old scarcity forced people to use their washing water again
every drop that ran away was watched closely then
the plenty of today makes a leak hard to notice
progress has done away with the carrying but hidden the waste
text: Households once drew their water from a shaft sunk in the ground or from a tank that caught the rain. You hauled the vessel up hand over hand, waited for the grit to settle at the bottom, then kept the supply cool in an earthenware pot standing out of the sun. Now a single movement at the household fitting brings it, and the flow owes nothing whatever to the bodily strength of whoever happens to be drawing. The difference between the two runs deeper than comfort. Scarcity used to impose a discipline of its own: the water from washing went on to the floor afterwards, and every drop that ran away was watched closely. Where supply feels endless, that watchfulness slackens, and a leak can seep quietly for weeks on end before anyone notices. Progress has done away with the carrying, then, and hidden the waste in the doing.

units: a kitchen drawer holds tools whose purpose is often forgotten
the one with a long handle and a deep bowl lifts hot liquid out
the perforated one holds the food back while the water runs away
its holes have to be narrow so that nothing is lost
the rack lets the plates dry in the air with no help from anyone
the citrus press keeps the juice clear of the flesh and traps the pips
the bendy blade scrapes the sides of a bowl clean without marking them
each tool answers to one particular movement
text: Open a kitchen drawer and you come upon a whole set of tools whose exact purpose has quietly slipped everyone's mind. Take the one with the long handle and the deep bowl: it is there to lift hot liquid out of the pan and keep your fingers well away from it. The perforated one holds the food back while the water runs off, and its holes want to be narrow, or half of what you cooked goes down with it. The draining rack goes about its business in its own good time — you stand the rinsed plates in it, and the air does the drying with no help at all from anyone. The citrus press keeps the juice clear of the flesh and traps the pips in the bottom of its little cup. The bendy blade scrapes the sides of a bowl clean without marking them. Each of these answers to one particular movement of the hand.

units: the incident happens just before the bread shop opens its doors
the cooking appliance can no longer reach the heat it needs
the woman in charge suspects the burner first and then the ignition sensor
the first batch comes out too pale and the display stays almost empty
a young member of staff decides to look at the flue opening
burnt crumbs of bread had packed the duct and starved the flame of air
clearing the duct takes about half an hour
the next batch comes out with its usual colour and smell
the woman in charge adds that check to her weekly habits
the story then travels round the neighbourhood by word of mouth
text: It began in the hour before the bread shop opened its doors: the oven would not come up to the heat it needed. The woman in charge suspected the burner first, then the sensor that governs the ignition. The first batch came out pale, with no crust worth the name, and the display stayed all but empty while people came in, left and came back. It was a young member of staff who thought to look at the flue opening. A mass of burnt crumbs had packed the duct tight and was quietly starving the flame of air. Clearing the whole of it took the better part of half an hour, dust and all. From the very next batch onwards the bread had its usual colour again and its usual smell. The woman in charge added that check to her weekly habits, and the story went round the neighbourhood by word of mouth.

units: the shoes must be kept away from any source of heat because the material dries out
the underside is to be brushed so that the caked mud comes off
hardened dirt holds water and eats away at the stitching
a lining that feels cold and slack shows the fabric has taken in water
crumpled paper serves to draw that damp out
the wax goes on sparingly and in circles
a thick coat never sinks in and spoils the look of the surface
polishing with a woollen cloth warms the wax and closes the pores
left untended the material splits where the foot bends
text: Because leather dries out when it is left standing beside anything warm, begin by moving the pair well away from every source of heat. Brush the underside next, so that the caked mud comes away from it, for hardened dirt holds water against the material and eats slowly away at the stitching that carries it. Slide a hand into the lining: cold and slack to the touch, it has drunk yesterday's rain, and crumpled paper pressed inside will draw that damp out of it. Then work in a little wax, sparingly and in patient circles, since a thick coat never sinks in and spoils the look of the surface. Leave it to settle, then bring it up with a woollen cloth; the rubbing warms the wax, which evens out and closes the pores. Left untended, the leather will split exactly where the foot bends, and nothing will mend it.

units: the body in charge of water has published a survey of its network
a sizeable share of the water sent out never reaches the homes
the older metal pipes crack because the ground beneath them shifts
the pressure swings that come at night add to those cracks
the first measure cuts the network into stretches that valves can seal off
meters read the overnight flow so that a loss can be spotted
a flow that does not drop away at night reveals a leak
the second measure brings the pressure down because hard pressure bursts pipes
a leak in a home counts for little beside a split main under the road
text: The body in charge of the water supply has put out a survey of the network it runs. The finding is a blunt one: a sizeable share of everything that goes into the mains never reaches the homes it was sent out to. Older metal pipes crack as the ground beneath them shifts about, and the pressure swings that come with the night hours work those cracks wider still. Two measures follow from this. The first cuts the network into short stretches that valves can seal off, with meters reading the overnight flow; where that flow fails to drop away in the small hours, water is going astray somewhere. The second brings the pressure down, since driving it hard is what bursts a pipe. A tap left dripping in a flat, the engineers add, counts for very little beside a split main under the road.

units: the space in front of the building is laid with uneven paving
tubs there hold green and sweet-smelling plants
a pale wall covering throws a soft light into the lower windows
the space at the back is covered with an even concrete surface
a wall without an opening blocks the view there
wooden seats and a water point invite people to stop in the first space
the second takes the bins and the delivery vehicles
one is meant to please and the other to serve
both spaces belong to the same building
text: The yard in front of the building is laid with paving that runs uneven underfoot, and tubs stand along its edges, holding ferns and sweet-smelling herbs. Pale render on the walls around it throws a soft light back into the windows of the lower floor. Behind the very same building the ground tells another story altogether: an even concrete surface runs from one side to the other, and a wall without a single opening in it blocks the view. The front yard asks you to stop a while, with wooden seats set against the brickwork and a water point for the planting. The one at the back takes the bins and the delivery vehicles, and nobody lingers there. One space is meant to please, the other to serve. Both belong to the same building, and the contrast tells you how a place shares out its uses.

units: the writer argues for mending a damaged appliance rather than replacing it
a spare part costs far less than an unused replacement
the money saved stays in the household budget
giving up a purchase avoids the digging out of material, the journey and the packaging
taking an appliance apart teaches how it works inside
that skill then passes on to the people around
mending is said to ask for a patience few people have
shared places offer the help of a volunteer and the loan of tools
the main difficulty comes from sealed manufacture that keeps appliances shut
text: Mending a damaged appliance rather than replacing it is a choice, and the case for it stands up on several separate grounds. Money, to start with: a spare part costs a mere fraction of an unused replacement, and what is not spent stays in the household budget. Materials, next: the digging out, the journey, the packaging, all of it goes when the purchase does not go through. Skill, last of all: whoever takes a casing apart learns how the thing works inside, and that understanding passes on in turn to the people around them. Mending asks for a patience that few people have, runs the objection. It forgets the shared places where a volunteer guides your hands and lends you the tools you lack. The one real difficulty is sealed manufacture, which keeps appliances shut against anyone opening them.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman who sells fresh produce began as a child at her mother's side
she sorted the crates before trading began
she could tell how ripe a fruit was from the sound it made in her palm
her first pitch was a few boards laid across trestles
later on a wooden counter under a canvas sheet took its place
she steers undecided buyers according to what they are after
one customer wants a fruit whose stone comes away easily
another asks for grapes with no seeds in them
she is now passing her trade to her niece, who takes notes
she says she never wrote anything down and trusts what her hands remember
text: The woman who sells fresh produce in the covered market began when she was very young, at her mother's side, sorting her way through the crates before trading began for the day. She could tell how ripe a plum was, she says, from the sound it made in her palm. Her first pitch was no more than a few boards laid across trestles; a wooden counter with a canvas sheet stretched over it took their place later on. She learned to steer the buyers who cannot make up their minds: this one wants a fruit whose stone comes away on its own, that one is after grapes with no seeds in them. Lately she has been passing the trade on to her niece, who takes down every tip in a notebook. She laughs and says that she herself never wrote a thing, and that her hands remember better than her head does.

units: the shared eating place stands in an old market building
one dish only is offered at each sitting
that limit brings about a quality rarely met
buying that is not spread thin gives access to vegetables grown in the open
the work starts very early in the day
the single broth can reduce to a thickness seldom found
the bread served alongside has a crisp crust
the hard surface of the room throws the voices back and makes talking difficult
nothing is laid on for those who will not eat root vegetables
text: The shared eating place set up in an old market building is worth the walk, and that comes down to one decision taken and held to: only one dish is offered at each sitting. From that limit comes a quality rarely met. Because the buying is never spread thin, vegetables grown out in the open can be had, and the work on them starts long before the day itself does. Because there is one broth and no other to be watched, it is left to reduce to a thickness you will seldom find. The ladle goes down into a soup that is thick and almost dark, and the bread served alongside has a crust that cracks under the tooth. The room, though, works against the meal: bare tiling throws the voices back, and talking soon turns into hard labour. Nothing is laid on either for anyone who will not eat root vegetables.
